title: C standard library overview and headers
learningObjectives: Explain that the C standard library provides portable interfaces declared by standard headers and implemented by the hosted or freestanding implementation as applicable.
Match common headers such as stdio.h, stdlib.h, string.h, math.h, ctype.h, time.h and stdint.h to their principal facilities.
Distinguish a declaration supplied by a header from the function definition supplied by the library implementation.
Include the correct header for each library identifier and avoid relying on undeclared functions or accidental transitive includes.
Check library preconditions, return values, object bounds and lifetime requirements when calling standard functions.
Identify when a facility is optional, implementation-defined, locale-sensitive or platform-specific rather than assuming universal behaviour.

understand.concept: The C standard library is a collection of specified types, macros and functions that programs can use through standard headers. A header such as <stdio.h> declares interfaces; the implementation provides the corresponding library definitions. Common headers include <stdlib.h> for conversions, allocation and process utilities; <string.h> for byte and string operations; <math.h> for mathematical functions; <ctype.h> for character classification and conversion; <time.h> for calendar time; and <stdint.h> for optional exact-width integer types and related limits.
understand.whyItMatters: Using standard interfaces avoids unnecessary reinvention and generally improves portability. However, every function has a contract: required headers, valid arguments, return-value rules, object sizes and lifetime constraints. A familiar function name does not make an invalid call safe.
understand.analogy: A standard header is like an interface catalogue: it tells a program which operations and types are available, while the library implementation supplies their behaviour.
understand.analogyLimit: Including a header does not guarantee that every optional facility exists on every implementation, nor does it validate arguments or make platform-specific behaviour portable.

explain.narrative:
A header provides declarations, macros and type definitions needed by the compiler. The implementation supplies the library code, often through the linker and runtime. Include the header that directly declares each identifier you use; do not rely on another header accidentally including it. The standard library is not one giant header, and a header is not generally a separately compiled source file.

Choose functions by contract. For example, strlen requires a valid null-terminated string; memcpy requires non-overlapping valid regions; malloc may return a null pointer; strtol reports conversion information through endptr and may set errno; printf format specifiers must match the argument types. Read the relevant function contract and check failure results.

Hosted C implementations provide the standard library facilities required for hosted programs. Freestanding implementations have a different required subset. Some headers and functions are optional or depend on implementation support. Compiler extensions and operating-system APIs should be identified as such rather than presented as ISO C.

examples.title: Use two standard headers for distinct jobs
examples.explanation: stdio.h declares printf and string.h declares strlen. The array is a valid null-terminated string, so strlen can find its length. Each identifier's declaring header is included directly.

examples.title: Check a library allocation result before use
examples.explanation: stdlib.h declares malloc and free; stdio.h declares the output functions. The program checks allocation before dereferencing and releases the allocated object exactly once.

practise.guidedTask: For each identifier printf, strlen, malloc, sqrt, isdigit and time, identify its declaring header, one important argument or return-value rule, and one possible failure or portability concern.
practise.independentTask: Write a small hosted C program that uses three standard headers for three different purposes. Include direct headers, validate inputs and library results, and explain the contract of every library call.
hints: Include the header that directly declares each identifier.
A declaration is not the same thing as the library's implementation.
Check whether a function expects a null-terminated string, a byte count or an element count.
Check allocation and conversion results before using them.
Do not assume optional facilities or platform APIs are ISO C.
Read the standard-library contract rather than guessing from a function name.

<string.h>

questions.explanation: stdio.h declares the standard input/output functions including printf.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a standard header?
options: It supplies declarations and macros for interfaces
It always contains the compiled machine code
It validates every function argument
It guarantees all optional extensions exist
questions.answer: It supplies declarations and macros for interfaces
questions.explanation: A header makes declarations visible; the implementation supplies library definitions.

questions.prompt: What must be true before calling strlen(s)?
options: s points to a valid null-terminated string
s points to any allocated bytes, even without a terminator
s must contain only digits
s must have been allocated by malloc
questions.answer: s points to a valid null-terminated string
questions.explanation: strlen searches for the terminating null character, so the string must be valid and terminated.

questions.prompt: Why should malloc's result be checked?
options: It can return a null pointer when allocation fails
It always returns one byte
It automatically initializes all bytes to zero
It frees earlier allocations
questions.answer: It can return a null pointer when allocation fails
questions.explanation: The caller must not dereference a null result and must manage the allocated object's lifetime.

options: Use standard interfaces and identify platform-specific extensions explicitly
Assume every compiler supports the same extensions
Rely on transitive header inclusion
Ignore implementation-defined limits
questions.answer: Use standard interfaces and identify platform-specific extensions explicitly
questions.explanation: ISO C interfaces are generally more portable than undocumented compiler or operating-system extensions.
